1261.event_title: Hachiko waits at Shibuya Station for his master
1261.event: Hachiko was an Akita dog owned by Hidesaburo Ueno, a professor of agricultural engineering at the University of Tokyo, and he used to wait at Shibuya Station for Ueno to come home. Ueno died suddenly at work on 21 May 1925, but Hachiko kept going to the station to wait for him for about ten more years. A statue of Hachiko now stands at Shibuya Station.
1261.explanation: Hachiko's daily vigil became a national symbol of faithful waiting for someone who has gone away.
1261.tie_back: The kural's heroine has worn out her eyes watching the road for her husband's return; Hachiko watched the station day after day for a master who never came back.
1261._accuracy_note: Next-best: the long daily watch for a return is a vivid match, but it is a dog's loyalty, not a wife's longing, and there is no marking of days.

1262.event_title: Edward I raises the Eleanor Crosses
1262.event: Eleanor of Castile, wife of King Edward I of England, died at Harby in Nottinghamshire on 28 November 1290. Her funeral procession travelled from Lincoln to Westminster in December, and Edward had a memorial cross built at each place where her body rested overnight, twelve in all. Three of the original crosses survive, at Geddington, Hardingstone and Waltham Cross.
1262.explanation: Rather than let his grief fade, the king set his love for his wife in stone along the road from Lincoln to London.
1262.tie_back: The kural's heroine refuses to forget her husband even though remembering costs her; Edward chose lasting remembrance of Eleanor over forgetting.
1262._accuracy_note: Next-best: a choice to keep remembering fits, but this is mourning after death by a husband, not a living wife's refusal to forget an absent husband.

1263.event_title: Douglas Mawson's extra year in Antarctica and Paquita Delprat's wait
1263.place: Commonwealth Bay, Antarctica, and Adelaide, Australia
1263.event: The geologist Douglas Mawson, engaged to Paquita Delprat, led the Australasian Antarctic Expedition from 1911. On a sledging journey in 1912 his companions Belgrave Ninnis and Xavier Mertz died, and Mawson struggled back alone to his base only to find that the relief ship Aurora had just left. He and six volunteers spent another winter there, he returned in 1914, and he and Paquita married on 31 March 1914 in Melbourne.
1263.explanation: Mawson went south in pursuit of discovery, and his fiancee had to wait more than two years, including an unplanned extra year, for his return.
1263.tie_back: The kural's heroine says her husband left in pursuit of achievement with only his resolve for company, and she lives on only in the hope of his return; Paquita Delprat waited through Mawson's long absence in just this situation.
1263._accuracy_note: Reasonable: the man leaving in pursuit of achievement and the woman waiting fits well, but the sources document her waiting only in outline, not her feelings.

1264.event_title: Alexander Selkirk is rescued after four years marooned
1264.place: Mas a Tierra, Juan Fernandez Islands (now Chile)
1264.event: After a quarrel with his captain in September 1704, the Scottish sailor Alexander Selkirk asked to be put ashore on the uninhabited island of Mas a Tierra, and he regretted the decision as soon as the ship sailed. During more than four years alone, two ships landed, but they were Spanish and he had to hide from their crews. In February 1709 he was picked up by an English ship commanded by Woodes Rogers.
1264.explanation: Selkirk's long wait for a friendly sail later helped inspire the story of Robinson Crusoe.
1264.tie_back: The kural's heroine sends her heart climbing from branch to branch to look out for her beloved's return; Selkirk's years of hope for a rescuing ship are a documented case of such watching.
1264._accuracy_note: Next-best only: eager hope for a return is the shared idea, but there is no beloved, and the sources do not describe him keeping a lookout.

1265.event_title: Natan and Avital Sharansky are reunited after twelve years
1265.event: Natan (Anatoly) Sharansky married Natalya Stiglitz in 1974, and she was allowed to emigrate to Israel the day after the wedding, expecting him to follow. He was arrested in March 1977 and sentenced to 13 years in prison and labour camps, while she, taking the name Avital, campaigned for his release from Jerusalem and abroad. He was freed in an East-West prisoner exchange on 11 February 1986 and arrived in Israel that day, where the couple were together again.
1265.explanation: Avital's long campaign was driven by a single wish: to see her husband again, after a marriage that had lasted only one day before their separation.
1265.tie_back: The kural's heroine asks only to see her husband until her eyes are full, sure that her pallor will then fade; Avital spent twelve years working toward exactly that sight.
1265._accuracy_note: Strong: a wife's years of longing to see her absent husband, ended by reunion, match closely; the sources do not describe the meeting itself in detail.

1266.event_title: Operation Homecoming brings American prisoners of war home
1266.place: Hanoi, Vietnam; Clark Air Base, Philippines; Travis Air Force Base, California
1266.event: Under the Paris Peace Accords, the first flight of Operation Homecoming carried 40 American prisoners of war out of Hanoi on 12 February 1973 to Clark Air Base in the Philippines. Flights continued into late March, and 591 prisoners returned to the United States, some after more than seven years in captivity. The first group of 20 reached Travis Air Force Base in California on 14 February 1973.
1266.explanation: After years of uncertainty for their families, the return flights ended long separations in a matter of days.
1266.tie_back: The kural's heroine says that if her husband comes back even for one day, all her grief will be gone; for the families of these prisoners, the day of return ended years of anxious waiting.
1266._accuracy_note: Next-best: return ending long grief fits, but the sources describe the flights rather than family reunions, and the kural is about a single wife and husband.

1267.event_title: Heloise writes to Abelard with reproach and love
1267.event: After Peter Abelard, then abbot of Saint-Gildas in Brittany, wrote an account of his misfortunes, Heloise, by then head of the convent of the Paraclete, wrote to him. In her letter she reproached him for not comforting her, either in person or by letter, since they had both entered religious life. In the same letter she declared that she had always loved him and that her heart still belonged to him.
1267.explanation: Heloise's letter is famous for holding complaint and devotion together in the same breath.
1267.tie_back: The kural's heroine cannot decide whether to sulk at her returning beloved, embrace him, or do both; Heloise's letter does both at once.
1267._accuracy_note: Reasonable: reproach mixed with love matches the 'sulk and embrace' dilemma, but there is no homecoming, and the couple had permanently separated.

1268.event_title: George Washington writes to Martha on taking command
1268.event: Days after the Continental Congress made him commander of the new army, George Washington wrote to his wife Martha from Philadelphia. He told her he had not sought the command, partly because he did not want to be parted from her and the family, and that he would find more real happiness in one month with her at home than in the most distant prospect abroad, even if his stay lasted seven times seven years. The letter is one of the very few between them to survive, because Martha is believed to have destroyed most of their correspondence.
1268.explanation: At the start of a long war, the new commander's private letter shows that his heart was at home with his wife.
1268.tie_back: The kural gives the husband's voice: let the king's campaign be won, and he will go home to feast with his wife; Washington, taking up command of a war, wrote that a month at home with Martha outweighed any glory abroad.
1268._accuracy_note: Strong: a man called to war longing to be home with his wife is almost the kural's scene, though Washington was the commander rather than a soldier serving a king.

1269.event_title: Anne Bradstreet's poems to her absent husband
1269.place: Massachusetts Bay Colony (now Massachusetts, United States)
1269.event: The Puritan poet Anne Bradstreet was married to Simon Bradstreet, whose duties as a colonial magistrate frequently took him away from home. She wrote love poems to him, including A Letter to her Husband, absent upon Publick employment, in which she pictures him as the sun and herself as chilled and numb while he stays away, begging him to return. The poems appeared in the Boston edition of her Several Poems in 1678.
1269.explanation: Bradstreet's poems are among the earliest records in American literature of a wife's longing during her husband's absences on public duty.
1269.tie_back: The kural says that for those waiting for a faraway beloved's return, one day passes like seven; Bradstreet describes the time of her husband's absence as a long cold season waiting for the sun to come back.
1269._accuracy_note: Reasonable: a wife's sense that time drags while her husband is away on duty fits well, though the poem does not count days.

1270.event_title: Mumtaz Mahal dies on Shah Jahan's Deccan campaign
1270.event: In 1631 Mumtaz Mahal, wife of the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan, accompanied him while pregnant on a military campaign in the Deccan. She died at Burhanpur after giving birth to the couple's fourteenth child. Her body was moved to Agra in January 1632, and work began there on the Taj Mahal as her tomb.
1270.explanation: The emperor's campaign went on, but the loss of his wife turned his energies to building one of the world's most famous monuments of grief.
1270.tie_back: The kural's husband, away on campaign, asks what use any reunion would be if his wife's heart broke and she died; Shah Jahan's campaign ended with exactly such a loss.
1270._accuracy_note: Next-best: a wife's death during her husband's campaign echoes the husband's fear, but she was travelling with him and died in childbirth, not of the grief of waiting.
